chunks: Al-ʿAlāʾ narrated from Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī, who said:
I asked Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who struck another man's head with a pickaxe, so his eyes flowed down onto his cheeks. Then the injured man sprang upon his striker and killed him.

So Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: "These two were both aggressors. I do not hold that qiṣāṣ applies against the one who killed the man, because he killed him at the time he killed him while he was blind, and the offense of a blind person is deemed a mistake. His ʿāqilah is liable for it; they are made to pay it over three years, in each year an installment. If the blind man has no ʿāqilah, then the diyah of what he committed is binding upon him from his own wealth, to be taken over three years. And the blind man may recourse against the heirs of the one who struck him for the diyah of his two eyes."

key_terms.جِنَايَتُهُ خَطَأٌ: his offense is treated as mistaken rather than intentional
key_terms.دِيَةُ مَا جَنَى: the blood money due for the injury or killing he caused
key_terms.عَاقِلَتُهُ: the male kin group responsible for paying blood money
key_terms.وَرَثَةِ ضَارِبِهِ: the heirs of the one who struck him

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a blinded man kills the person who assaulted him in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a fiqh ruling on injury, homicide, and liability when a man is blinded and then kills his attacker. Imam Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام rules that qiṣāṣ does not apply in this case, treats the blind person's offense as mistaken, assigns diyah through the ʿāqilah or his wealth, and affirms his right to claim compensation for the loss of his eyes.
